title: Ports, protocols & purpose
summary: Understand the conversation behind a connection.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: An IP address identifies a network interface, while a transport port helps deliver traffic to the intended service. A browser reaching an encrypted website normally uses HTTPS on port 443. DNS normally answers name-resolution queries on port 53. SSH commonly uses port 22 for encrypted remote terminal access. These are conventional defaults, not guarantees: an administrator can move a service to another port.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: TCP establishes a connection, numbers data, and retransmits missing segments so applications receive an ordered byte stream. UDP sends independent datagrams without providing those same delivery guarantees. This lower transport overhead suits applications that manage timing or recovery themselves. DNS commonly uses UDP for ordinary queries but also uses TCP when appropriate; avoid treating a service as permanently tied to only one transport. When diagnosing connectivity, check the destination address, service port, transport, and any firewall rule together.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
